{{Short description|Measure of the influence of a data point in regression analysis}}
In [[statistics]], '''Cook's distance''' or '''Cook's ''D''''' is a commonly used estimate of the [[Influential observation|influence]] of a data point when performing a least-squares [[regression analysis]].<ref>{{cite book |last1= Mendenhall |first1= William |last2=Sincich |first2=Terry |title=A Second Course in Statistics: Regression Analysis |edition=5th |year=1996 |publisher=Prentice-Hall |location=Upper Saddle River, NJ |isbn=0-13-396821-9 |page=422 |quote=A measure of overall influence an outlying observation has on the estimated <math>\beta</math> coefficients was proposed by R. D. Cook (1979). Cook's distance, ''D<sub>i</sub>'', is calculated...}}</ref> In a practical [[ordinary least squares]] analysis, Cook's distance can be used in several ways: to indicate influential data points that are particularly worth checking for validity; or to indicate regions of the design space where it would be good to be able to obtain more data points. It is named after the American statistician [[R. Dennis Cook]], who introduced the concept in 1977.<!-- the expression "Cook's Distance" appears at least as early as 1979 --><ref>{{cite journal
  | last=Cook |first=R. Dennis
  | title=Detection of Influential Observations in Linear Regression
  | journal=Technometrics
  | volume=19 |issue=1 |pages= 15–18
  |date=February 1977
  | publisher=[[American Statistical Association]]
  | mr=0436478
  | doi=10.2307/1268249
  | jstor=1268249
 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
  | last=Cook |first=R. Dennis
  | title=Influential Observations in Linear Regression
  | journal=[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]]
  | volume=74 |issue=365 |pages=169–174
  |date=March 1979
  | publisher=American Statistical Association
  | mr=0529533
  | doi=10.2307/2286747
  | jstor=2286747
 | hdl=11299/199280
  | hdl-access=free
  }}</ref>

==Definition==
Data points with large [[Residual (statistics)|residuals]] ([[outlier]]s) and/or high [[Leverage (statistics)|leverage]] may distort the outcome and accuracy of a regression. Cook's distance measures the effect of deleting a given observation. Points with a large Cook's distance are considered to merit closer examination in the analysis.

For the [[algebraic expression]], first define

: <math>\underset{n \times 1}{\mathbf{y}} = \underset{n \times p}{\mathbf{X}} \quad \underset{p \times 1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \quad + \quad \underset{n \times 1}{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}</math>

where <math>\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}\left( 0, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I} \right)</math> is the [[Errors and residuals|error term]], <math>\boldsymbol{\beta} = \left[ \beta_{0} \, \beta_{1} \dots \beta_{p-1} \right]^{\mathsf{T}}</math> is the [[coefficient matrix]], <math>p</math> is the number of covariates or predictors for each observation, and <math>\mathbf{X}</math> is the [[design matrix]] including a constant. The [[least squares]] estimator then is <math>\mathbf{b} = \left( \mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{X} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{y}</math>, and consequently the fitted (predicted) values for the mean of <math>\mathbf{y}</math> are

:<math>\mathbf{\widehat{y}} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{X} \left( \mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{X} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{y}</math>

where <math>\mathbf{H} \equiv \mathbf{X} ( \mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}}</math> is the  [[projection matrix]] (or hat matrix). The <math>i</math>-th diagonal element of <math>\mathbf{H} \,</math>, given by <math>h_{ii} \equiv \mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf{T}} ( \mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_i</math>,<ref>{{cite book |first=Fumio |last=Hayashi |title=Econometrics |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2000 |pages=21–23 |isbn=1400823838 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QyIW8WUIyzcC&pg=PA21 }}</ref> is known as the [[Leverage (statistics)|leverage]] of the <math>i</math>-th observation. Similarly, the <math>i</math>-th element of the residual vector <math>\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{\widehat{y\,}} = \left( \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H} \right) \mathbf{y}</math> is denoted by <math>e_i</math>.

Cook's distance <math>D_i</math> of observation <math>i \; (\text{for } i = 1, \dots, n)</math> is defined as the sum of all the changes in the regression model when observation <math>i</math> is removed from it<ref name=mathworks>{{cite web|url=http://se.mathworks.com/help/stats/cooks-distance.html|title=Cook's Distance}}</ref>

: <math>
D_i = \frac { \sum_{j=1}^n \left( \widehat{y\,}_j - \widehat{y\,}_{j(i)} \right)^2 } {p s^2}
</math>

where ''p'' is the rank of the model (i.e., number of independent variables in the design matrix) and <math>\widehat{y\,}_{j(i)}</math> is the fitted response value obtained when excluding <math>i</math>, and <math>s^2 =  \frac{\mathbf{e}^\top \mathbf{e}}{n-p} </math> is the [[mean squared error]] of the regression model.<ref>{{cite web |title=Statistics 512: Applied Linear Models |work=Purdue University |url=https://www.stat.purdue.edu/~jennings/stat514/stat512notes/topic3.pdf#page=9 |access-date=2016-03-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161130150249/http://www.stat.purdue.edu/~jennings/stat514/stat512notes/topic3.pdf#page=9 |archive-date=2016-11-30 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Equivalently, it can be expressed using the leverage<ref name=mathworks/> (<math>h_{ii}</math>):

: <math>D_i = \frac{e_i^2}{p s^2}\left[\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}\right]  . </math>

==Detecting highly influential observations==
There are different opinions regarding what cut-off values to use for spotting highly [[influential observations|influential points]]. Since Cook's distance is in the metric of an [[F-distribution|''F'' distribution]] with <math>p</math> and <math>n-p</math> (as defined for the design matrix <math>\mathbf{X}</math> above) degrees of freedom, the median point (i.e., <math>F_{0.5}(p,n-p)</math>) can be used as a cut-off.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Bollen |first1= Kenneth A. |author-link= Kenneth A. Bollen |last2= Jackman |first2= Robert W. |year= 1990 |chapter= Regression Diagnostics: An Expository Treatment of Outliers and Influential Cases |editor-last= Fox |editor-first= John |editor2-last= Long |editor2-link= J. Scott Long |editor2-first= J. Scott |title= Modern Methods of Data Analysis |pages= [https://archive.org/details/modernmethodsofd0000unse/page/266 266] |location= Newbury Park, CA |publisher= Sage |isbn= 0-8039-3366-5 |chapter-url= https://archive.org/details/modernmethodsofd0000unse/page/266 }}</ref> Since this value is close to 1 for large <math>n</math>, a simple operational guideline of <math>D_i>1</math> has been suggested.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cook |first1=R. Dennis |last2=Weisberg |first2=Sanford |author-link2=Sanford Weisberg |year=1982 |title=Residuals and Influence in Regression |location=New York, NY |publisher=Chapman & Hall |isbn=0-412-24280-X |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MVSqAAAAIAAJ |hdl=11299/37076}}</ref>

Note that in general the Cook's distance  does not  measure correctly the influence of observations.
<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Myung Geun|last1=Kim|title=A cautionary note on the use of Cook's distance|journal=Communications for Statistical Applications and Methods|date=31 May 2017|issn=2383-4757|pages=317–324|volume=24|issue=3|doi=10.5351/csam.2017.24.3.317|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Relationship to other influence measures (and interpretation)==

<math>D_i</math> can be expressed using the leverage<ref name=mathworks/> (<math>0 \leq h_{ii} \leq 1</math>) and the square of the ''internally'' [[Studentized residual]] (<math>0 \leq t_i^2</math>), as follows:

: <math>
\begin{align}
D_i &= \frac{e_i^2}{p s^2} \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2} = \frac{1}{p} \cdot \frac{e_i^2}{{1 \over n-p} \sum_{j=1}^n \widehat{\varepsilon\,}_j^{\,2} (1-h_{ii})} \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}} \\[5pt] 
&= \frac{1}{p} \cdot t_i^2 \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}} . 
\end{align}
</math>

The benefit in the last formulation is that it clearly shows the relationship between <math>t_i^2</math> and <math>h_{ii}</math> to <math>D_i</math> (while p and n are the same for all observations). If <math>t_i^2</math> is large then it (for non-extreme values of <math>h_{ii}</math>) will increase <math>D_i</math>. If <math>h_{ii}</math> is close to 0 then <math>D_i</math> will be small, while if <math>h_{ii}</math> is close to 1 then <math>D_i</math> will become very large (as long as <math>t_i^2 > 0</math>, i.e.: that the observation <math>i</math> is not exactly on the regression line that was fitted without observation <math>i</math>).

<math>D_i</math> is related to [[DFFITS]] through the following relationship (note that <math>{\widehat{\sigma} \over \widehat{\sigma}_{(i)}} t_i = t_{i(i)}</math> is the ''externally'' studentized residual, and <math>\widehat{\sigma}, \widehat{\sigma}_{(i)}</math> are defined [[Studentized residual#Internal and external studentization|here]]):

: <math>
\begin{align}
D_i &= \frac 1 p \cdot t_i^2 \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}} \\
&= \frac{1}{p} \cdot \frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{(i)}^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2} \cdot \frac{\widehat{\sigma}^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_{(i)}^2} \cdot t_i^2 \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}} 
= \frac{1}{p} \cdot \frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{(i)}^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2} \cdot \left(t_{i(i)} \sqrt{\frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}}}\right)^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{p} \cdot \frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{(i)}^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2} \cdot \text{DFFITS}^2
\end{align}
</math>

<math>D_i</math> can be interpreted as the distance one's estimates move within the confidence ellipsoid that represents a region of plausible values for the parameters.{{Clarify|date=July 2010}} This is shown by an alternative but equivalent representation of Cook's distance in terms of changes to the estimates of the regression parameters between the cases, where the particular observation is either included or excluded from the regression analysis.

An alternative to <math>D_i</math> has been proposed. Instead of considering the influence a single observation has on the overall model, the statistics <math>S_i</math> serves as a measure of how sensitive the prediction of the <math>i</math>-th observation is to the deletion of each observation in the original [[data set]]. It can be formulated as a weighted [[linear combination]] of the <math>D_{j}</math>'s of all data points. Again, the [[projection matrix]] is involved in the calculation to obtain the required weights:

: <math>
S_i = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^n \left(\widehat{y}_i-{\widehat{y}_i}_{(j)}\right)^2}{ps^2 h_{ii}} = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac { h_{ij}^2 \cdot D_j} { h_{ii} \cdot h_{jj} } = \sum_{j=1}^n \rho_{ij}^2 \cdot D_j
</math>

In this context, <math>\rho_{ij}</math> (<math>\leq 1</math>) resembles the correlation between the predictions <math> \widehat{y\,}_i</math> and <math> \widehat{y\,}_j</math>{{refn|group=lower-alpha|The indices <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> are often interchanged in the original publication as the [[projection matrix]] <math>\mathbf{H}</math> is symmetric in ordinary linear regression, i.e., <math>h_{ij} = h_{ji}</math>. Since this is not always the case, e.g., in weighted linear regression, the indices have been written consistently here to account for potential asymmetry and thus allow for direct usage.{{sfn|Peña|2005|p=2}}}}.<br>
In contrast to <math>D_{i}</math>, the distribution of <math>S_{i}</math> is asymptotically normal for large sample sizes and models with many predictors. In absence of outliers the [[expected value]] of <math>S_{i}</math> is approximately <math>p^{-1}</math>. An influential observation can be identified if

: <math>
\left| S_i - \operatorname{med}(S) \right| \geq 4.5 \cdot \operatorname{MAD}(S)
</math>

with <math>\operatorname{med}(S)</math> as the [[median]] and <math>\operatorname{MAD}(S)</math> as the [[median absolute deviation]] of all <math>S</math>-values within the original data set, i.e., a robust measure of location and a [[robust measure of scale]] for the distribution of <math>S_i</math>. The factor 4.5 covers approx. 3 [[standard deviations]] of <math>S</math> around its centre.<br>
When compared to Cook's distance, <math>S_i</math> was found to perform well for high- and intermediate-leverage outliers, even in presence of masking effects for which <math>D_{i}</math> failed.<ref>{{cite journal
  | first = Daniel
  | last = Peña
  | title = A New Statistic for Influence in Linear Regression
  | journal = Technometrics
  | volume = 47 |issue = 1 |pages = 1–12
  | date = 2005
  | publisher = [[American Society for Quality]] and the [[American Statistical Association]]
  | doi = 10.1198/004017004000000662
| s2cid = 1802937
 }}</ref><br>
Interestingly, <math>D_i</math> and <math>S_i</math> are closely related because they can both be expressed in terms of the matrix <math>\mathbf{T}</math> which holds the effects of the deletion of the <math>j</math>-th data point on the <math>i</math>-th prediction:

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \mathbf{T} = \left[\begin{matrix} \widehat{y}_{1}-{\widehat{y}_{1}}_{\left(1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{1}-{\widehat{y}_{1}}_{\left(2\right)} & \widehat{y}_{1}-{\widehat{y}_{1}}_{\left(3\right)} & \cdots & \widehat{y}_{1}-{\widehat{y}_{1}}_{\left(n-1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{1}-{\widehat{y}_{1}}_{\left(n\right)} \\ \widehat{y}_{2}-{\widehat{y}_{2}}_{\left(1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{2}-{\widehat{y}_{2}}_{\left(2\right)} & \widehat{y}_{2}-{\widehat{y}_{2}}_{\left(3\right)} & \cdots & \widehat{y}_{2}-{\widehat{y}_{2}}_{\left(n-1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{2}-{\widehat{y}_{2}}_{\left(n\right)} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots &\ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \widehat{y}_{n-1}-{\widehat{y}_{n-1}}_{\left(1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{n-1}-{\widehat{y}_{n-1}}_{\left(2\right)} & \widehat{y}_{n-1}-{\widehat{y}_{n-1}}_{\left(3\right)} & \cdots & \widehat{y}_{n-1}-{\widehat{y}_{n-1}}_{\left(n-1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{n-1}-{\widehat{y}_{n-1}}_{\left(n\right)} \\ \widehat{y}_{n}-{\widehat{y}_{n}}_{\left(1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{n}-{\widehat{y}_{n}}_{\left(2\right)} & \widehat{y}_{n}-{\widehat{y}_{n}}_{\left(3\right)} & \cdots & \widehat{y}_{n}-{\widehat{y}_{n}}_{\left(n-1\right)} & \widehat{y}_{n}-{\widehat{y}_{n}}_{\left(n\right)} \end{matrix}\right] \\ \\
&\ \ = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{H} \left[\begin{matrix} e_1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & e_2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & e_{n-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & e_n \end{matrix}\right] \left[\begin{matrix} \frac 1 {1-h_{11}} & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac 1 {1-h_{22}} & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac 1 {1-h_{n-1,n-1}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & \frac 1 {1-h_{nn}} \end{matrix}\right]
\end{align}
</math>

With <math>\mathbf{T}</math> at hand, <math>\mathbf{D}</math> is given by:

: <math>
\mathbf{D} = \left[\begin{matrix} D_1 \\ D_2 \\ \vdots \\ D_{n-1} \\ D_n \end{matrix}\right] = \frac 1{ps^2} \operatorname{diag}\left(\mathbf{T}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{T}\right) = \frac 1 {ps^2} \operatorname{diag} \left(\mathbf{G} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{H} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{G} \right) = \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{M})
</math>

where <math>\mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{H}</math> if <math>\mathbf{H}</math> is [[Symmetric matrix|symmetric]] and [[Idempotence|idempotent]], [[Projection matrix#Properties|which is not necessarily the case]]. In contrast, <math>\mathbf{S}</math> can be calculated as:

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \mathbf{S} = \left[\begin{matrix} S_1 \\ S_2 \\ \vdots \\ S_{n-1} \\ S_n \end{matrix}\right] = \frac{1}{ps^2} \mathbf{F} \operatorname{diag} \left(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{T}^{\mathsf{T}}\right) = \frac{1}{ps^2} \left[\begin{matrix} \frac{1}{h_{11}} & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{h_{22}} & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{1}{h_{n-1n-1}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & \frac{1}{h_{nn}} \end{matrix}\right] \operatorname{diag} \left(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{T}^{\mathsf{T}}\right) \\ \\
&\ \ = \frac{1}{ps^2} \mathbf{F} \operatorname{diag} \left( \mathbf{H} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{G} \mathbf{G} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) = \mathbf{F} \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{P})
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A})</math> extracts the [[main diagonal]] of a square matrix <math>\mathbf{A}</math>. In this context, <math>\mathbf{M} = p^{-1} s^{-2} \mathbf{G} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{H} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{G}</math> is referred to as the influence matrix whereas <math>\mathbf{P} = p^{-1} s^{-2} \mathbf{H} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{G} \mathbf{G} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{T}} </math> resembles the so-called sensitivity matrix. An [[Eigenvalues|eigenvector analysis]] of <math>\mathbf{M}</math> and <math>\mathbf{P}</math> - which both share the same eigenvalues – serves as a tool in outlier detection, although the eigenvectors of the sensitivity matrix are more powerful.<ref>{{cite book
  | first = Daniel
  | last = Peña
  | title = Springer Handbook of Engineering Statistics 
  | pages = 523–536
  | editor-first = Hoang
  | editor-last = Pham
  | date = 2006
  | publisher = Springer London
  | doi = 10.1007/978-1-84628-288-1
  | isbn = 978-1-84628-288-1
  | s2cid = 60460007
 | url = https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007/978-1-84628-288-1_28
}}</ref>

==Software implementations==
Many programs and statistics packages, such as [[R (programming language)|R]], [[Python (programming language)|Python]], [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]], etc., include implementations of Cook's distance.

{| class="wikitable sortable"
|-
! Language/Program !! Function !! Notes
|-
| [[Stata]] || <code>predict, cooksd</code>  || See [https://www.stata.com/manuals/rregresspostestimation.pdf]
|-
| [[R (programming language)|R]] || <code>cooks.distance(model, ...)</code>  || See [https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/influence.measures.html]
|-
| [[Python (programming language)|Python]] || <code>CooksDistance().fit(X, y)</code>  || See [https://www.scikit-yb.org/en/latest/api/regressor/influence.html#cook-s-distance]
|-
| [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]] || <code>cooksdistance(model, ...)</code>  || See [https://juliastats.org/GLM.jl/stable/]
|}

==Extensions==

High-dimensional Influence Measure (HIM) is an alternative to Cook's distance for when <math>p>n</math> (i.e., when there are more predictors than observations).<ref>[https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aos/1384871348 High-dimensional influence measure]</ref> While the Cook's distance quantifies the individual observation's influence on the least squares regression coefficient estimate, the HIM measures the influence of an observation on the marginal correlations.

A general class of influence measures for ''multivariate'' linear models with several response variable has been given by Barrett & Ling (1992).<ref>General classes of influence measures for multivariate regression, Journal of the American Statistical Association (1992), 87(417), 184–191, https://www.jstor.org/stable/i314301</ref>
These are implemented for R in the '''mvinfluence''' package
<ref>{{cite web | title=Influence Measures and Diagnostic Plots for Multivariate Linear Models | url=https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/ }}</ref>
